BUSINESS BASICS

Learn the words before you use them.

Business can sound harder than it is because people often explain simple ideas with complicated words. This section starts with the things you will keep seeing across every country and every industry.

Revenue is not profit.

If a brand sells a jacket for $150, the $150 is revenue. It is not automatically money the owner gets to keep. Fabric, manufacturing, shipping, staff, rent, payment fees, marketing and taxes can all come out before there is profit.

The idea to rememberSales tell you how much came in. Profit asks what was left after the business paid its costs.

Cash flow is a different problem.

A business can look profitable on paper and still struggle to pay its bills. Imagine a retailer that has sold a large order but will not be paid for 60 days while its supplier wants payment this week. The business has a sale, but it may still be short on cash.

The idea to rememberProfit asks whether the business makes money. Cash flow asks whether it has the money at the moment it needs it.

Equity means ownership.

When a founder gives an investor 10% of the company for capital, the investor is not simply lending money. They are receiving part of the ownership. That can affect future decisions, voting rights and what happens when the company raises more money.

The idea to rememberInvestment is not always debt. Sometimes the price of getting capital is sharing ownership.

Why does the company structure matter?

An LLC, corporation, partnership or local equivalent is not just a different registration label. The structure can affect who owns the business, who manages it, how liability works, how investors enter and which tax rules apply.

The idea to rememberThe legal structure is part of the business model because it shapes how the company is allowed to operate.

Trademark, copyright and design are not the same.

A brand name and logo, a photograph or piece of writing, and the appearance of a product can raise different intellectual-property questions. Protecting one does not automatically protect all the others.

The idea to rememberBefore asking “How do I protect my brand?”, ask what exactly you are trying to protect.

Tax is usually a system, not one number.

Depending on the country, a business may deal with taxes on company income, sales or consumption, employees and payroll, property, imports or other activities. The tax that matters depends on what the business actually does.

The idea to rememberNever compare countries using one tax rate and assume you have compared their whole business environment.

FOLLOW THE MONEY

See what happens to one sale.

One of the easiest ways to understand a business is to stop looking at the company as a logo and follow one transaction from the customer backwards.

Customer pays→Business receives revenue→Costs are paid→Taxes & obligations→Profit or reinvestment

Imagine a $100 fashion sale.

The customer pays $100. That is the starting point, not the finish line. If the garment cost $28 to make, shipping cost $7, the payment platform kept a fee, marketing helped generate the sale, and the business has staff and storage costs, the amount left is already much smaller.

Then the tax rules of the place where the business operates can matter. Some taxes are collected from the customer and passed on; others are costs of the business itself. That distinction is why “the tax rate” is never the whole story.

Now change the business.

A software company might have almost no physical shipping cost but spend heavily on developers and cloud infrastructure. A restaurant has food waste, rent, staff and local operating rules. A manufacturer may have machinery, inventory and a long payment cycle.

The same $100 of revenue can therefore mean very different things in different industries.

Why location changes the picture.

Where the company sells, employs people, stores goods or imports products can introduce different tax and regulatory questions. This is one reason Themis asks you to look at the country and, where useful, the city or region rather than treating a country as one giant business environment.

The question to carry into every country.

Do not start with “What is the tax rate?” Start with “Where does the money move?” Once you know who pays whom, where the product travels, where employees work and where the company earns its revenue, the relevant taxes and rules become much easier to understand.

Where do you want to look?

“If I actually built my company here, what would happen?”

Start with why the market matters, then follow the practical reality: how money moves, what the company needs, which taxes can apply, which permissions matter, and what can make the market difficult.

NOT A SALES PITCH

A market can be attractive and still be expensive, regulated or operationally difficult. The point is to understand the trade-offs before making a decision.

COUNTRY DEPTH

Why does business feel different here?

Go one layer deeper than country facts. Each market has its own business logic: where companies tend to operate, how industries are organized, what makes expansion complicated, and which questions deserve attention first.

CHOOSE A MARKET

See the business logic behind the map.

AMERICAS

The U.S. is a collection of business environments, not one single market.

A company can be incorporated in one state while its people, stores, customers or operations are elsewhere. That makes location a practical business question, not just a paperwork question.

MarketLarge domestic market with strong regional differences.StructureFederal, state and local layers can all matter.IndustriesTechnology, finance, consumer, media and professional services have distinct ecosystems.ExpansionMoving into another state can introduce a new set of registrations and rules.
The useful question is often: where will the business actually operate?

What should you notice?

The difference between where a company is formed and where it does business is one of the clearest ways to see why geography matters in business.

State choice can affect the practical operating environment.
City and region can matter for talent, customers and costs.
Sector-specific rules can sit on top of general company rules.

Educational overview. Country rules, licensing, tax and market conditions change; use the relevant official authority when researching an actual business decision.

HOW MONEY WORKS

See the business before you see the tax.

Tax is not a headline percentage. It sits inside the business model: what you sell → what you spend → what counts as taxable income → what obligations appear next.

ILLUSTRATIVE SCENARIO · SINGAPORE

“I am building a small company. What could the numbers look like?”

Chargeable income*S$200,000
Illustrative CITS$34,000
After illustrative CITS$166,000

*Educational illustration using a simplified model. Singapore's headline corporate income tax rate is 17% of chargeable income. Qualifying new start-ups can receive exemptions on specified portions of the first S$200,000 of normal chargeable income for their first three consecutive Years of Assessment. Actual tax depends on the company's facts, deductions, exemptions and current rules.

01 · REVENUE

What are you actually earning?

Separate sales from profit. A company can have high revenue and still have little taxable income after allowable expenses.

02 · COSTS

What does it take to operate?

People, rent, software, logistics, professional services and financing can change the economics long before tax enters the conversation.

03 · TAX

What does the rule actually tax?

Look for the tax base, filing obligations, exemptions and the conditions attached to them—not just the headline rate.

THE REALITY CHECK

The hardest part may not be incorporation.

Getting a company on a register is only one moment. The harder question is whether the business can operate legally, affordably and sustainably once it exists.

“What could make this business harder than it looks from the outside?”

Choose a country →
BUSINESS × LAW

Law does not arrive after the business. It is inside the business.

A company does not usually wake up one morning and suddenly “need a lawyer.” Legal questions appear while ordinary business decisions are being made: choosing an owner, signing with a supplier, hiring someone, naming a product, taking customer data, importing goods, advertising a service or expanding into another country.

THE QUESTION

“What changes because this business is a legal entity operating in a real place?”

Business explains what the company is trying to do. Law helps define what the company is allowed to do, what it promises to other people, who owns what, and what happens when something goes wrong.

Think of law as part of the system.

It can change cost, timing, ownership, risk, contracts, hiring, marketing and even whether an activity can happen at all.

01
THE COMPANY

Who actually owns the business?

Before a company sells anything, someone owns it. The legal structure determines how ownership is held and can affect management, liability, investment and what happens if the business grows or changes hands.

Business connection: A founder bringing in an investor may be giving away part of the company rather than simply borrowing money.
What law adds: Ownership, voting rights, governance and liability have legal consequences.
02
CONTRACTS

Who promised what to whom?

A business rarely works alone. It buys materials, hires software providers, rents space, uses logistics companies and sells to customers. Each relationship can create promises that matter if one side does not perform.

Example: A fashion brand agrees to buy 2,000 garments from a manufacturer. Price, delivery, quality, payment and what happens to defective products are not just business preferences—they can become contractual obligations.
03
INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY

What belongs to the business?

The valuable thing may not be the building or the inventory. It might be a brand name, logo, software code, photograph, design, invention, database or creative work.

Business connection: The more recognizable a brand becomes, the more valuable its identity can be.
What law adds: Different kinds of intellectual property protect different things. Owning one does not automatically mean owning all the others.
04
PEOPLE

When does hiring become a legal relationship?

Hiring is a business decision because people do the work. It is also a legal relationship involving pay, working conditions, leave, termination and other obligations that depend on the country and sometimes the region.

Example: A restaurant opening in a new city cannot simply copy the employment arrangement it used somewhere else. Local employment rules may change the contract, payroll process and operating cost.
05
CUSTOMERS

What are you promising the customer?

A sale is more than money changing hands. Product descriptions, pricing, returns, warranties, subscriptions and advertising can all shape what the customer is entitled to expect.

Business connection: A brand wants its marketing to be persuasive.
What law adds: Consumer-protection rules can limit misleading claims and establish rights that businesses must respect.
06
PERMISSIONS

Can the business legally do this activity?

Some businesses can begin with relatively few sector-specific permissions. Others operate in areas where regulators, licences, registrations or approvals are central to the business model.

Compare: A clothing brand and a financial-services company may both be “companies,” but the legal questions around what they are allowed to do can be completely different.
07
DATA

What happens to information about people?

A website can collect names, email addresses, payment information, location data or behavioural information. A business may also share data with cloud providers, payment processors or other partners.

Business connection: Data can make a product more useful and a marketing system more effective.
What law adds: Privacy and data-protection rules can affect what may be collected, why it may be used, how it is stored and what rights people have.
08
CROSS-BORDER

What changes when the business crosses a border?

A company can be incorporated in one country, employ people in another, manufacture somewhere else and sell to customers around the world. That is normal for many modern businesses—and it creates more than one legal environment.

Example: A Turkish founder may own a company incorporated abroad while its team, customers or warehouse are in other countries. The question is no longer simply “Where is my company registered?” but “Where is the business actually operating?”
THE SAME LAW, DIFFERENT BUSINESS

Why sector matters

Fashion

Brand protection, supplier agreements, product information, imports, advertising, returns and designs can all become relevant.

Technology

Software ownership, SaaS contracts, privacy, fundraising, employment and licensing can sit at the centre of the business.

Food & Hospitality

Premises, food safety, employees, suppliers, customer complaints and local operating permissions can shape the model.

Professional Services

Client agreements, confidentiality, professional rules, liability and sector-specific permissions may matter more than physical infrastructure.

WHAT TO REMEMBER

Do not ask only “What law applies to companies?” Ask: What is this business doing, where is it doing it, who is involved, what is being promised, and what is being exchanged? Those questions lead you toward the legal issues that actually matter.

Educational content only · Rules vary by country, sector and current legislation.
REAL BUSINESS CASES

Look closely at the decisions behind real businesses.

A company can look simple from the outside. The interesting part is usually hidden underneath: where it is incorporated, how it grows, who carries the risk, who owns the intellectual property, and what changes when the business gets bigger. Founder Stories

Before the company had a name, there was a person figuring it out.

Founder Stories are not celebrity profiles. They are business decisions in context: what problem existed, what the first version looked like, what did not work, and what the founder learned before the company became obvious in hindsight.

WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS

You are allowed to start before you feel ready.

Almost every famous company looks obvious in hindsight. The early version usually was not. Someone had a half-formed idea, learned something they did not know, made a decision with incomplete information, changed direction, or simply kept going long enough to see a better version of the idea. The point of these stories is not to turn founders into heroes. It is to show the work behind the outcome — and to remind you that your first version is allowed to be unfinished.

CONSUMER · USA

Sara Blakely — Spanx

A simple clothing problem became a product business. The early story shows how customer observation can matter more than having a huge starting budget.

YOUR TURN

Do not ask only, “How did they win?”

Ask: What did they not know yet? What did the first version look like? Which assumption turned out to be wrong? Who helped them? What changed when the business became bigger? Those questions make a founder story useful instead of inspirational wallpaper.

ABOUT THE PROJECT

Why I built Themis.

Themis started with a simple frustration: legal learning can become a list of cases, terms and rules without showing the business decisions underneath them. I wanted to build something that connected those two worlds.

Themis Library grew around legal research and learning. Themis Business grew from the next question: what changes when the same business idea enters a different country, market or legal system?

That is why the two projects belong together. A case can explain a rule, but the business behind that rule explains why the rule matters. A country can look attractive on paper, but the way money moves, companies are structured, products are sold and people are employed can change the picture completely.

I built Themis as a learning project, not as a substitute for a lawyer, accountant or official authority. The goal is to make the first layer of research easier to understand—and to point students toward the primary sources when they want to go further.
